subtopic_detail: GDM initial dietary trial before pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old G1P0 at 27+3 weeks in the antenatal diabetes clinic. Her booking BMI was 31 kg/m2 and her mother was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 45. She was screened at 26 weeks with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test after skipping first trimester HbA1c.

OGTT results: fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), one hour 11.0 mmol/L (<10.0), two hour 8.9 mmol/L (<8.5). She meets ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes.

She reports no polydipsia, polyuria or infections. She is asymptomatic with no vision changes. She has been offered diabetes educator and dietitian input which she can attend within one week.

Today's dating scan showed appropriate for gestational age foetus with no polyhydramnios. Blood pressure and proteinuria are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC, foetal HR 148 /min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, symphyseal fundal height 27 cm, foetal movements reported normal
data_table.Investigations: As above; HbA1c today 5.6% (<5.7 non-pregnant), urea and creatinine normal, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in four weeks to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
options.rationale: A single positive OGTT meeting ADIPS criteria makes the diagnosis and delaying management for a repeat test exposes mother and foetus to four weeks of untreated hyperglycaemia; there is no diagnostic need for confirmation. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily now and titrate up to 2 g daily over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first line at diagnosis in the absence of severe hyperglycaemia; ADIPS calls for a trial of medical nutrition therapy with self monitoring first, with metformin or insulin added if glucose targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Start subcutaneous long acting insulin at 0.2 units/kg at bedtime now with morning glucose review
options.rationale: Insulin is first line pharmacotherapy when nutrition therapy fails or when there is severe hyperglycaemia at diagnosis; the OGTT here is mildly elevated and a trial of medical nutrition therapy is indicated first. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Refer to diabetes educator and dietitian and start four times daily home glucose monitoring with review
options.rationale: ADIPS first line management of newly diagnosed GDM is medical nutrition therapy, physical activity and home glucose self monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets (fasting under 5.0 and two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L) are not met within one to two weeks. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

options.text: Plan a category 1 induction of labour at 39 weeks now without additional glucose monitoring in the interim
options.rationale: Delivery timing decisions in GDM depend on glycaemic control, foetal growth and complications during ongoing pregnancy, not on the diagnosis alone; this bypasses the need for glucose management and monitoring in the interim. (Source: RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnostic criteria for GDM on a 75 g OGTT are fasting 5.1, one hour 10.0, two hour 8.5 mmol/L (any one). First line management is medical nutrition therapy from a dietitian, structured physical activity and home glucose self monitoring four times daily targeting fasting under 5.0 and one hour post prandial under 7.4 (or two hour under 6.7). Pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) is added if targets are not met within 1-2 weeks, or immediately for severe hyperglycaemia or foetal macrosomia. Insulin remains first line pharmacotherapy in AU, with metformin used in specific settings after counselling on placental transfer.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1h 10.0, 2h 8.5 mmol/L
Glucose targets on treatment: fasting under 5.0, 1h post prandial under 7.4, 2h under 6.7
MNT first, pharmacotherapy if targets missed at 1-2 weeks
Insulin first line pharmacotherapy in AU, metformin alternative
explanation.pearls: Metformin crosses the placenta but the MiG trial and long term follow up show broadly reassuring neonatal outcomes; AU practice still starts with insulin more often than metformin, unlike some UK pathways.

stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 30 year old woman for her six week postnatal check after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a healthy term baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and plans to continue for at least six months. She wants to resume contraception before she and her partner become sexually active again.

She had one previous pregnancy that ended in a first trimester miscarriage. She has no history of migraine, venous thromboembolism, hypertension, cardiac or liver disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m2 and blood pressure today is 118/74. She smokes five cigarettes daily and has cut down from twenty during the pregnancy.

She does not want an intrauterine device at this stage due to needle phobia and wants a method she can start today. She has not resumed periods.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Well healed episiotomy, uterus involuted, no pelvic tenderness, no varicose veins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to prescribe today?

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today after signed consent and post procedure observation
options.rationale: The implant is safe and effective but requires a subdermal insertion which she declined for the same reason as the IUD; the pill matches her stated preference and MEC category 1 status. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today with a three month review to reassess breastfeeding
options.rationale: MEC AU category 3 (risks outweigh benefits) for combined pill in the first six weeks postpartum in a breastfeeding woman due to venous thromboembolism and lactation concerns; category 2 after 6 weeks but not first choice while breastfeeding. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular given today with review in 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA is safe in breastfeeding but requires an injection which she declined for other reasons and has a slower return to fertility and bone mineral density concerns with long use; the pill better matches her preference. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Advise lactational amenorrhoea method alone until she has fully weaned her infant off breastfeeding
options.rationale: LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months, and even then has a failure rate of about 2% in typical use; she needs a defined method as she does not want to rely on breastfeeding pattern alone. (Source: FSRH postnatal contraception guideline)

options.text: Progestogen only pill starting today with no additional precautions if fully breastfeeding and amenorrhoeic
options.rationale: MEC AU category 1 for progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum; it does not affect lactation and can be started immediately with no additional precautions if within 21 days postpartum or amenorrhoeic. It is also compatible with smoking under 15/day if under 35. (Source: MEC AU 2021; FSRH progestogen only pill guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: MEC AU categorises contraception in breastfeeding women. Progestogen only methods (pill, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUS) are all category 1 or 2 from any time postpartum and do not impair lactation. Combined hormonal methods are category 3 in the first six weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (VTE and lactation concerns) and category 2 from 6 weeks onwards. If she declines devices, the progestogen only pill is a category 1 first choice that can start today. Contraception should be discussed by six weeks postpartum because ovulation can return before menses.
key_points: MEC AU 1: progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum
MEC AU 3: combined pill in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding
Ovulation may return before menses so contraception before day 21 if not breastfeeding
LAM is 98% effective only if exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months
explanation.pearls: The progestogen only pill window in AU is often quoted as 3 hours for older levonorgestrel pills and 12 hours for desogestrel and drospirenone - check the product prescribed.

stem:
You are the O and G registrar seeing a 34 year old woman in the early pregnancy clinic six weeks after her third consecutive first trimester miscarriage. Her first pregnancy at 24 ended in a miscarriage at 8 weeks with a normal karyotype on products of conception. Her second at 26 miscarried at 10 weeks with a similar karyotype result. The most recent miscarriage at 12 weeks was managed medically with no complications.

She reports one episode of provoked deep vein thrombosis after a long haul flight two years ago that was treated with three months of rivaroxaban and has not recurred. She smokes ten cigarettes daily.

She is not currently pregnant and her partner has fathered another child in a previous relationship. Recent parental karyotypes were normal. A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound showed a normal uterine cavity with no septum. Thyroid function and prolactin are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, cardiovascular examination normal, no lower limb swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide future pregnancy care?

options.text: Empirical low molecular weight heparin from a positive pregnancy test without further diagnostic workup
options.rationale: Empirical LMWH in the absence of documented antiphospholipid syndrome or heritable thrombophilia has not been shown to reduce miscarriage in trials (SPIN, ALIFE); prescribing it exposes her to needle burden and bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ALIFE trial NEJM 2010)

options.text: Hysteroscopy with septum resection to exclude uterine cavity abnormality missed on ultrasound
options.rationale: A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound has already shown a normal cavity with no septum and no further imaging is needed unless the ultrasound was unclear; empirical resection has no evidence of benefit without a documented lesion. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody screen: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 GP1 IgG and IgM
options.rationale: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage workup includes antiphospholipid antibody screening after 3 or more first trimester losses; diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome requires a positive test confirmed on repeat 12 weeks later, and treatment (aspirin plus low molecular weight heparin) reduces subsequent loss. Her provoked DVT is not itself diagnostic without APL. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ISTH APS classification criteria 2023)

options.text: Send further parental karyotypes and array comparative genomic hybridisation on parental blood samples
options.rationale: Parental karyotypes have already returned normal and repeat testing is not indicated; array comparative genomic hybridisation is a cytogenetic tool for products of conception rather than parental blood in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

options.text: Advise assisted reproductive technology with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy screening
options.rationale: PGT-A has not been shown to improve live birth rate in couples with unexplained recurrent miscarriage and normal parental karyotypes; empirical use adds cost, cycle burden and does not address a potentially treatable cause like APS. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive first trimester losses or two or more with any second trimester loss) warrants structured workup: pelvic imaging for uterine anomaly, parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibody screen and thyroid and prolactin. In this case the cavity is normal, karyotypes are normal and endocrine screen is normal, so the outstanding test is APL antibodies. APS diagnosis needs a positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti beta 2 glycoprotein 1 antibody confirmed at 12 weeks. Treatment with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from a positive pregnancy test improves live birth rate in obstetric APS.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage: 3 or more first trimester OR 2 or more with any second trimester loss
Workup: pelvic imaging, parental karyotype, APL antibodies, thyroid, prolactin
APS diagnosis: positive APL confirmed at 12 weeks
Empirical LMWH in unexplained recurrent miscarriage is not evidence based
explanation.pearls: The ISTH APS classification criteria 2023 use domain scoring so a single positive result is not enough - two positive results 12 weeks apart, at least one at moderate to high titre, is needed to confirm.

subtopic_detail: ICP delivery timing by bile acid tier
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old G2P1 at 35+4 weeks referred by her midwife for severe generalised itch that started three weeks ago and is worse at night. It affects her palms and soles most. She has no rash on examination beyond scratch marks. Her first pregnancy was affected by intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy at 34 weeks and she was induced at 37 weeks with a live vigorous infant.

Today's bloods show a fasting serum bile acid of 108 micromol/L (<10) rising from 62 last week. ALT is 168 U/L (<45), GGT is 92 U/L (<50). Total bilirubin and INR are within normal limits.

Ultrasound today shows a singleton cephalic foetus with estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile, normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler within normal limits. Cardiotocograph is reassuring at 140 bpm baseline with normal variability and accelerations. She has been counselled about foetal risks and started on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily last week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC, foetal HR 140 /min
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations without primary rash, no jaundice, uterus soft with normal fundal height, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Fasting bile acids 108 micromol/L (was 62), ALT 168 U/L, GGT 92 U/L, INR 1.0, viral hepatitis screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Continue expectant management until spontaneous labour or 40 weeks gestation with weekly bloods
options.rationale: Bile acids over 100 micromol/L carry an absolute stillbirth risk that rises from 37 weeks onwards; expectant management until spontaneous labour or 40 weeks is inconsistent with contemporary AU and UK practice for severe ICP. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

options.text: Plan expedited delivery at 36 weeks by induction of labour with continuous intrapartum CTG monitoring
options.rationale: RCOG and RANZCOG endorsed bile acid stratification identifies severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 micromol/L as carrying a stillbirth risk that is materially higher than background from 36 weeks; delivery at 36 weeks is recommended with continuous intrapartum CTG. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section this evening under general anaesthesia for foetal indication
options.rationale: There is no acute foetal compromise on CTG, Doppler or growth to warrant category 1 delivery tonight; the timing decision here is elective planning at 36 weeks, not emergency birth. (Source: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.text: Plan induction at 39+0 weeks and continue outpatient bile acid monitoring every week until delivery
options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks is appropriate for mild ICP with bile acids under 40 micromol/L; severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 requires earlier delivery to reduce stillbirth risk. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

options.text: Discontinue ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat bile acids in one week before deciding delivery timing
options.rationale: PITCHES showed UDCA does not reduce foetal composite outcomes but many centres continue it for maternal itch; stopping it does not change delivery timing which is driven by the peak bile acid tier. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; PITCHES Lancet 2019)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is stratified by peak bile acid: mild (under 40), moderate (40-99) and severe (100 or more micromol/L). Stillbirth risk rises sharply above 100 micromol/L from about 37 weeks. Contemporary guidance recommends delivery at 36 weeks for severe ICP, 38-39 weeks for moderate and 39-40 weeks for mild disease. UDCA improves maternal pruritus and biochemistry but the PITCHES trial did not show reduction in composite foetal outcomes; it is not a substitute for delivery timing. Continuous intrapartum CTG is recommended given the small but definable stillbirth risk.
key_points: Severe ICP: bile acids 100 or more, deliver at 36 weeks
Moderate ICP: 40-99, deliver 38-39 weeks
Mild ICP: under 40, deliver 39-40 weeks
UDCA improves itch but does not remove need for timed delivery
explanation.pearls: Peak bile acids drive the plan - so ongoing measurement matters even after treatment starts, because tier can escalate.

sources.label: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

stem:
You are the O and G registrar reviewing a 27 year old G1P0 in the early pregnancy assessment unit with two days of mild left iliac fossa pain and a small amount of dark brown vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was seven weeks ago. She has never had an ectopic before and has no history of pelvic infection, tubal surgery or IUD use.

Ultrasound today shows an empty uterus, a 2.4 cm mass in the left adnexum without a foetal pole or foetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid. Serum beta hCG today is 1820 IU/L. She is haemodynamically stable and pain scores 3/10 on paracetamol.

She lives 20 minutes from the hospital, has reliable transport and a partner at home. She has no chronic liver, renal or haematological disease. Full blood count and liver and renal function are within normal limits. She has been counselled about medical, surgical and expectant management options in a shared decision making conversation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed, minimal dark blood in the vault
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 1820 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-160), platelets 258 x10^9/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Uterine evacuation with dilation and curettage to establish the location of the pregnancy definitively
options.rationale: The pregnancy is not intrauterine on ultrasound so curettage of an empty uterus is not indicated and can delay treatment of the extrauterine pregnancy; location has already been established sonographically. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy on the current admission under general anaesthesia and postoperative care
options.rationale: Surgical management is preferred for haemodynamic instability, severe pain, contraindications to methotrexate or when medical management fails; in a stable woman meeting all methotrexate criteria, medical management avoids surgical morbidity and preserves the contralateral tube. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy on the current admission with tubal preservation and postoperative followup
options.rationale: Salpingostomy carries a persistent trophoblast rate around 4-15% and adds no live birth benefit over salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy; it is not preferred over methotrexate in a stable woman meeting medical criteria. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly outpatient beta hCG monitoring only and no immediate intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for women with declining beta hCG under 1000, an asymptomatic clinical picture and clear evidence of resolution; a rising or stable hCG at 1820 with a visible adnexal mass has too high a rupture risk to observe without treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 single dose with beta hCG on day 4 and day 7 and clear return advice
options.rationale: This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, no contraindications and normal bloods. Single dose methotrexate has resolution rates around 85-90% in appropriately selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS; eTG: Ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic pregnancy are: hCG under 5000 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemodynamic instability, reliable follow up, no contraindications (liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression) and normal baseline blood tests. Single dose regimen is methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with beta hCG on day 4 and day 7; success is a fall of at least 15% between days 4 and 7. Failure or rise triggers a second dose or surgery. Anti-D immunoglobulin should be considered if Rh negative.
key_points: hCG threshold for methotrexate: under 5000 IU/L
Mass size threshold: under 3.5 cm
Requires no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow up
Contraindications: liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L (or the presence of cardiac activity, or mass at or above 3.5 cm, or instability, or contraindications to methotrexate) - not the older 3000 IU/L figure.

subtopic_detail: MCDA twin pregnancy - TTTS surveillance and delivery
stem:
You are the maternal foetal medicine registrar reviewing a 31 year old G2P1 at 26+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy for a fortnightly ultrasound. Chorionicity was established at 12 weeks by lambda sign absence and thin intertwin membrane. Anatomy scan at 20 weeks was normal in both twins with concordant growth. Two weeks ago twin A had estimated foetal weight on the 45th centile with maximum vertical amniotic pocket 3.8 cm and twin B on the 40th centile with 4.2 cm pocket.

Today twin A has estimated foetal weight on the 25th centile with maximum vertical pocket 1.4 cm and an empty bladder that has not filled across a 30 minute scan window. Twin B has estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile with maximum vertical pocket 9.6 cm and a distended bladder. Umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end diastolic flow in twin A and normal flow in twin B. Ductus venosus and middle cerebral artery Doppler are normal in both.

Both twins have reassuring cardiotocograph tracings. She has no contractions and cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC, foetal HRs A 148 /min B 152 /min
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, no contractions, cervix long and closed on transvaginal scan
data_table.Investigations: As above; full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Selective foetal reduction of twin A by bipolar cord occlusion during elective foetal medicine intervention
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for cases with severe growth restriction and imminent demise of the donor threatening the recipient by exsanguination through anastomoses, or major structural anomaly; laser is offered before reduction as it preserves both twins where possible. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Amnioreduction alone with a further scan in one week to reassess Quintero staging and Doppler
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is inferior to laser for TTTS at 16-26 weeks (Eurofoetus trial: survival of at least one twin 76% laser vs 51% amnioreduction) and delays definitive therapy; if a foetal therapy centre is inaccessible amnioreduction is a temporising measure at best. (Source: Eurofoetus trial NEJM 2004)

options.text: Administer betamethasone and plan delivery within 48 hours by caesarean section for foetal indication
options.rationale: At 26+3 weeks with reassuring CTGs and normal ductus venosus flow, immediate delivery carries very high extreme prematurity morbidity that is worse than the risk of transferring for laser therapy; delivery is reserved for irretrievable Doppler deterioration or foetal distress. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Urgent referral to a foetal therapy centre for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
options.rationale: TTTS stage III (Quintero: oligohydramnios pocket under 2 in donor, polyhydramnios pocket over 8 in recipient, empty donor bladder plus abnormal Doppler with absent end diastolic flow) at 16-26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of intertwin anastomoses; laser improves at least one twin survival compared with amnioreduction (Eurofoetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is at the outer margin and referral is time critical. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement; ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

options.text: Increase surveillance to weekly biometry and Doppler without intervention on both twins for two weeks
options.rationale: TTTS with abnormal Doppler is a treat now diagnosis, not a watch and wait; without laser the composite mortality of untreated stage III TTTS at this gestation approaches 80-90%. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates 10-15% of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies and is staged by the Quintero classification: stage I (oligo-poly), II (donor bladder not visible), III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), IV (hydrops), V (demise). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated by fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the intertwin anastomoses which has been shown superior to serial amnioreduction (Eurofoetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is right at the upper margin of the classic laser window; urgent transfer to a foetal therapy centre is time critical.
key_points: MCDA chorionicity mandates fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks
Quintero staging: I oligo-poly, II bladder gone, III abnormal Doppler, IV hydrops, V demise
Stage II+ at 16-26 weeks: fetoscopic laser preferred over amnioreduction
Delivery is a fallback when laser is not feasible or when demise is imminent
explanation.pearls: The absence of the lambda sign at 11-13 weeks confirms monochorionicity - a determination that cannot be reliably made retrospectively later in pregnancy, which is why every twin pregnancy must have chorionicity documented at the nuchal scan.

stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man brought to the emergency department by his family for four days of decreased sleep, pressured speech and grandiose plans to launch three business ideas. He is euphoric and irritable when interrupted. He has an established diagnosis of bipolar I disorder made two years ago after a manic episode that responded to olanzapine and he was maintained on quetiapine 300 mg at night. Six weeks ago he self ceased quetiapine when he moved cities.

He has no medical comorbidities and no history of renal, thyroid or cardiac disease. He denies substance use and a urine drug screen is negative. He has no suicidal ideation. He agrees informally to admission for stabilisation. He has taken no medication in six weeks and his last lithium level was never measured because he has never trialled lithium.

Routine bloods including thyroid function, urea and electrolytes and beta hCG (not applicable) are within normal limits. Fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ECG shows sinus rhythm rate 92 with normal QTc.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert and agitated, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions of business empire, insight limited, no formal thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function all within normal limits; ECG normal sinus rhythm normal QTc

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally every four hours as the sole pharmacotherapy without another mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a role for adjunctive sedation and sleep in acute mania but do not treat the underlying mood episode; monotherapy leaves the manic process unopposed. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily titrated up to 100 mg over two weeks with weekly outpatient mood review
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate or worsen mania and is not indicated for acute mania; it is contraindicated in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Lithium carbonate started at 500 mg at night with plasma level check at day 5 targeting 0.8 to 1.0
options.rationale: RANZCP mood disorder guideline lists lithium and second generation antipsychotics as first line for acute mania; lithium has the strongest evidence for both acute mania and long term prophylaxis, and normal renal and thyroid function make it safe to initiate. Target level for acute mania is 0.8-1.0 mmol/L. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021; eTG: Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated up to 200 mg over the next six weeks with weekly rash review
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is effective for bipolar depression maintenance but not for acute mania and has a slow titration required to reduce SJS risk; it does not treat the acute episode. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as monotherapy with GP review at two and four weeks for tolerance check
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in acute mania and can precipitate rapid cycling; SSRIs are not first line for a manic presentation. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

explanation.summary: Acute mania is treated with either lithium or a second generation antipsychotic as first line under RANZCP guidance. Lithium has the strongest evidence for acute and prophylactic treatment and is appropriate in a young man with normal renal and thyroid function who has not previously trialled it. Target acute mania level is 0.8-1.0 mmol/L with careful hydration counselling and avoidance of NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides. Combination lithium plus antipsychotic is used for severe or partial response. Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in mania.
key_points: First line acute mania: lithium OR second generation antipsychotic
Lithium acute mania target level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L
Antidepressant monotherapy contraindicated in bipolar disorder
Lamotrigine used for bipolar depression maintenance, not acute mania
explanation.pearls: Lithium takes 5-7 days to reach steady state and effect is not immediate; short term benzodiazepines are often given alongside for behavioural control while lithium reaches therapeutic level.

sources.label: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman with an established diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder for three years. Her intrusive contamination thoughts drive four to six hours of daily hand washing that has left the skin on her hands cracked and painful. She has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for six weeks having been up titrated from 50 mg. She is engaged with a psychologist for exposure and response prevention weekly for the last two months and is completing home exercises.

She reports mild improvement in urge intensity but no reduction in washing frequency or duration. She has had no significant side effects, no suicidal ideation and no sexual dysfunction concerns. She has never taken any other psychiatric medication and is not on other prescription medication. She does not use recreational substances and drinks two standard drinks weekly.

Her weight is stable, her sleep is adequate and her mood is euthymic in between episodes of anxiety. Family history is negative for bipolar disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Excoriated skin over dorsum of both hands, no jaundice, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated at this review; recent full blood count and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Titrate sertraline up to 200 mg daily over four weeks and review response and tolerance at eight weeks
options.rationale: OCD typically requires higher SSRI doses than depression and a longer trial (10-12 weeks); RANZCP and NICE recommend titrating to the maximum tolerated licensed dose (sertraline 200 mg) before declaring treatment failure. Sertraline 100 mg is a mid dose in OCD terms. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance; NICE OCD guideline CG31)

options.text: Add risperidone 1 mg daily as an adjunct antipsychotic and continue current sertraline dose unchanged
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for OCD that has failed maximal tolerated SSRI trial at 10-12 weeks, particularly for tic-related or partial response OCD; adding it now bypasses full SSRI titration. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Switch sertraline for a benzodiazepine to reduce anxiety before compulsive acts and monitor tolerance
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not indicated in OCD, are habit forming with tolerance, and do not address the underlying obsessive process; SSRIs and ERP remain first line. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Stop sertraline and switch to venlafaxine 75 mg daily with review of anxiety symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: SNRIs like venlafaxine have weaker evidence than SSRIs in OCD and would not be preferred without completing a maximal SSRI trial first; switching now abandons a treatment that has been shown effective. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Refer directly for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and continue sertraline at 100 mg
options.rationale: rTMS is a treatment option for treatment resistant OCD after failure of maximal SSRI trials and ERP, not a first step at six weeks on 100 mg sertraline. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

explanation.summary: OCD responds to SSRIs at higher doses and needs a longer trial than depression. RANZCP recommends titrating to the maximum tolerated licensed dose (sertraline 200 mg, fluoxetine 80 mg, paroxetine 60 mg, escitalopram 40 mg) and waiting 10-12 weeks before declaring treatment failure. Exposure and response prevention is combined with SSRI first line. Antipsychotic augmentation (risperidone or aripiprazole) or switching to clomipramine is second line after maximal SSRI trial. rTMS and deep brain stimulation are options in refractory cases.
key_points: OCD needs higher SSRI doses and longer trials than depression
Sertraline goes to 200 mg, fluoxetine to 80 mg, escitalopram to 40 mg for OCD
Combine SSRI with exposure and response prevention
Antipsychotic augmentation only after maximal SSRI trial fails
explanation.pearls: Escitalopram 40 mg for OCD exceeds the TGA general 20 mg maximum but is an accepted higher licensed dose for OCD specifically - documenting the OCD indication in the notes matters when the pharmacy queries.

stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35 year old man on clozapine for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has been stable for three years with much reduced positive symptoms after trials of risperidone and olanzapine did not achieve remission. He attends his monthly clozapine clinic today for his four weekly review and blood collection.

His full blood count today returns with a neutrophil count of 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), down from 2.6 four weeks ago. His platelets and haemoglobin are within normal limits. He is clinically well without fever, sore throat or infective symptoms. He has been fully adherent with medication and denies smoking cessation, new medications, or substance use.

He lives independently, is engaged in supported employment and reports his best psychosocial functioning in a decade. He is very keen to remain on clozapine and asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, no oral thrush, no pharyngeal erythema, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (was 2.6), white cells 4.2 x10^9/L (4-11), haemoglobin 145 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the full blood count twice weekly until stable
options.rationale: Under AU Clopine and Clozaril monitoring protocols this result is classified as amber (neutrophils 1.0-1.5 x10^9/L in non-benign neutropenia populations) - clozapine is continued with twice weekly FBC until stable or a red zone (under 1.0) is reached, at which point clozapine is ceased and haematology involved. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol; TGA clozapine risk management plan)

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and admit for urgent GCSF and daily haematology inpatient review this week
options.rationale: Amber zone neutropenia (1.0-1.5) does not mandate cessation; stopping clozapine after three years of stability without a red zone result exposes the patient to relapse of severe treatment resistant psychosis and is not required by the AU protocol. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol)

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and continue four weekly full blood count monitoring in the community
options.rationale: Neutropenia risk with clozapine is idiosyncratic and not consistently dose related; reducing the dose does not reliably increase neutrophils and may sacrifice symptom control. Increasing monitoring frequency is the correct amber zone response. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol)

options.text: Switch to olanzapine 20 mg daily now and cease clozapine monitoring bloods from this appointment onwards
options.rationale: He is on clozapine because olanzapine failed to control psychosis; switching abandons the treatment that has given him three stable years and is not required by the amber zone result. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol)

options.text: Add lithium 500 mg daily as neutrophil count booster and continue current four weekly monitoring at clinic
options.rationale: Lithium has been used empirically for clozapine associated neutropenia in some centres but is not standard AU practice and adds toxicity risk; the immediate amber zone response is increased monitoring, not adding lithium. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol)

explanation.summary: AU clozapine monitoring uses a green (neutrophils 2.0 or more), amber (1.0-1.9 in non-benign ethnic neutropenia populations) and red (under 1.0) zone system, with weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks then monthly. An amber zone result continues clozapine but increases FBC to at least twice weekly until stable green or falls to red. A red zone (neutrophils under 1.0) mandates immediate cessation of clozapine, haematology involvement and GCSF if febrile. Rechallenge is possible only through the special access scheme after severe cases.
key_points: Green zone: neutrophils 2.0 or more, continue monthly monitoring
Amber zone: 1.0-1.9, continue clozapine but check FBC twice weekly
Red zone: under 1.0, cease clozapine and involve haematology
First 18 weeks require weekly FBC before switching to monthly
explanation.pearls: Benign ethnic neutropenia (common in African, Middle Eastern and some Mediterranean populations) has different thresholds - the AU protocol allows enrolment with baseline neutrophils 1.5 or more in these patients with haematology sign off.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman on the general medical ward on day 3 of admission for dehydration. Her family brought her in after three days of refusing to eat, drink or speak. She has a background of bipolar I disorder with previous depressive episodes but no prior psychosis. She stopped her lithium six months ago.

On assessment she lies motionless staring at the ceiling, does not respond to voice or handshake, and holds her arm in the position it is placed after passive movement. Her lips move silently and she echoes single words the nurse says. She has not eaten, drunk or opened her bowels since admission and has required IV fluids. Vital signs are stable with no fever.

Medical workup including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, CRP, urinalysis and non contrast CT head is unremarkable. A collateral history from her partner confirms no recent medication changes and no substance use.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, staring, waxy flexibility, echolalia, no rigidity, no tremor, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, CRP, urinalysis and non contrast CT head all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give oral diazepam 10 mg three times daily and reassess catatonic features at the next ward round
options.rationale: Oral diazepam has slow and unpredictable absorption in a mute immobile patient and is not the recognised challenge test; IV lorazepam gives a reliable diagnostic response within minutes. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Start intramuscular olanzapine 5 mg and observe her mental state over the next 24 hours on the ward
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen or precipitate malignant catatonia and are second choice at best in catatonia; lorazepam or ECT are first line and antipsychotics should be avoided until catatonia is treated. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Restart lithium at 500 mg at night as long term mood stabiliser prophylaxis and community review
options.rationale: Long term prophylaxis considerations do not treat the acute catatonic state, which is the immediate life threatening concern given dehydration risk; acute treatment with lorazepam or ECT is required first. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture for suspected autoimmune encephalitis before starting any acute treatment
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis (particularly anti NMDA receptor) can present with catatonia and may be considered if the presentation is atypical or investigations point to it, but workup should not delay a lorazepam challenge which is diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenous and reassess Bush Francis catatonia rating at 15 minutes
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) both confirms the diagnosis of catatonia and is the first line treatment; a positive response defined as at least 50% improvement in Bush Francis score at 5-15 minutes confirms catatonia and predicts response to continued lorazepam. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance; Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome diagnosed by DSM 5 with three or more features from a set including mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia, negativism, stereotypy and grimacing. It can occur in mood disorders, psychotic disorders and general medical conditions including autoimmune encephalitis. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, reassess Bush Francis score at 5-15 minutes) is both diagnostic and first line treatment; ECT is second line or first line for malignant or refractory catatonia. Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are avoided until it is treated.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge: 1-2 mg IV, reassess Bush Francis score at 5-15 minutes
First line ongoing treatment: lorazepam 2 mg three times daily titrated up
ECT is second line or first line for malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is treated (worsening risk)
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia) shares features with neuroleptic malignant syndrome - both are treated with lorazepam and ECT rather than continued antipsychotic exposure.
